items.title: Two Dilemmas Close the Case Against No Cause At All

items.zh: 今應問彼：汝宿住念，為念無體？為念自我？若念無體，無體之法未曾串習，未曾經識，而能隨念，不應道理。若念自我，計我先無，後欻然生，不應道理。
items.en: One should press those relying on meditative memory: does your memory of past abodes take something with no substance as its object, or does it take a self as its object? If it takes something with no substance, then recollecting something never previously experienced or become familiar with makes no sense. If it takes a self as its object, then holding that this self first did not exist and then suddenly arose from nothing makes no sense either.

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？一切世間內外諸物種種生起，或欻然生起，為無因耶？為有因耶？若無因者，種種生起欻然而起，有時不生，不應道理。若有因者，我及世間無因而生，不應道理。
items.en: Further, to those relying on ordinary reasoning: what do you actually intend — does the world's varied array of internal and external phenomena, and their apparently sudden arising, occur without any cause, or with a cause? If without any cause, then their arising sometimes and not arising at other times makes no sense — an uncaused event should occur constantly and indiscriminately, not selectively. If with a cause, then insisting the self and the world arise without any cause at all makes no sense.

items.zh: 如是念無體故，念自我故，內外諸物不由因緣種種異故，由彼因緣種種異故，不應道理。是故此論非如理說。
items.en: Thus, because memory has no substance, because of remembering one's own self, because inner and outer things do not vary without causes and conditions, and because they vary according to those causes and conditions, it does not accord with reason. Therefore this doctrine is not soundly reasoned.

items.title: The Twelfth Doctrine: Total Annihilation at Death — Seven Cases, Already Previewed

items.zh: 斷見論者，謂如有一，若沙門、若婆羅門，起如是見，立如是論：乃至我有麁色四大所造之身，住持未壞，爾時有病、有癰、有箭。若我死後，斷壞無有，爾時我善斷滅。如是欲界諸天，色界諸天，若無色界空無邊處所攝，乃至非想非非想處所攝，廣說如經。
items.en: The doctrine of annihilation: there are certain renunciants or brahmins who hold such a view and establish such a doctrine — that as long as I possess this coarse body made of the four great elements, and it remains intact, unbroken, I am subject to sickness, to festering wounds, to the sting of resentment. But once I die, this body is utterly destroyed and ceases to exist, and at that time I am perfectly, completely extinguished. So too — stated in full as in the sūtra — for the desire realm's gods, the form realm's gods, and those belonging to the formless realm's sphere of infinite space, up through the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

items.zh: 謂說七種斷見論者作如是計。問：何因緣故，彼諸外道起如是見，立如是論？答：由教及理故。教如前說。理者，謂如有一，為性尋思，乃至廣說。
items.en: This is what those who teach the seven kinds of annihilationism hold. Question: For what reason do those non-Buddhist teachers hold this view and establish this doctrine? Answer: Because of scripture and reasoning. Scripture is as explained before. Reasoning means that someone is a speculator by nature, and so on at length.

items.zh: 彼如是思：若我死後復有身者，應不作業而得果異熟。若我體性一切永無，是則應無受業果異熟。觀此二種，理俱不可。是故起如是見，立如是論：我身死已，斷壞無有，猶如瓦石，若一破已、不可還合；彼亦如是，道理應知。
items.en: They reason thus: were I to have a further body after death, then I would obtain a ripened karmic result without having performed the corresponding deed — this seems wrong. Yet were my own nature to be utterly, permanently nonexistent even now, then there would be no one at all to receive the ripened result of karma already performed — this too seems wrong. Weighing these two positions, they find neither acceptable, and so arrive at this view and establish this doctrine: that once my body dies, it is utterly destroyed and ceases to exist — like a shattered tile or stone that can never be put back together — and it should be understood that I am exactly the same.

items.title: Aggregates Never Actually Stop, and "Self" Was Never There to Be Annihilated

items.zh: 今應問彼：汝何所欲？為蘊斷滅？為我斷滅耶？若言蘊斷滅者，蘊體無常，因果展轉生起不絕，而言斷滅，不應道理。
items.en: One should press them: what do you actually intend — is it the aggregates that are annihilated, or is it a self? If you say the aggregates are annihilated, then note that the aggregates, being impermanent, continue on through an unbroken chain of cause and effect — so calling this "annihilation" makes no sense.

items.zh: 若言我斷，汝先所說麁色四大所造之身有病、有癰、有箭，欲界諸天，色界諸天，若無色界空無邊處所攝，乃至非想非非想處所攝，不應道理。如是若蘊斷滅故，若我斷滅故，皆不應理。是故此論非如理說。
items.en: If you say a self is annihilated, then what you described earlier — a coarse body made of the four elements, subject to sickness, boils, and arrows; the desire realm's gods; the form realm's gods; and those of the formless realm, belonging to the sphere of infinite space up through the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception — makes no sense. Thus, whether the aggregates are said to be annihilated, or a self is said to be annihilated, neither position holds up — and so this doctrine is not a soundly reasoned teaching.

items.title: The Thirteenth Doctrine: Two Kinds of "Emptiness" Gone Wrong

items.zh: 空見論者，謂如有一，若沙門、若婆羅門，起如是見，立如是論：無有施與，無有愛養，無有祠祀，廣說乃至世間無有真阿羅漢。
items.en: The doctrine of the empty view: there are certain renunciants or brahmins who hold such a view and establish such a doctrine — that there is no such thing as giving, no such thing as caring for one's elders, no such thing as making offerings, and so on in full detail, up to and including the claim that there exists no genuine arhat anywhere in the world.

items.zh: 復起如是見，立如是論：無有一切諸法體相。
items.en: There are also some who, further, hold this view and establish this doctrine: that no phenomenon whatsoever has any real characteristic or nature at all.

items.zh: 問：何因緣故，彼諸外道起如是見，立如是論？答：由教及理故。教如前說。理者，謂如有一，為性尋思，乃至廣說。
items.en: Question: For what reason do those non-Buddhist teachers hold this view and establish this doctrine? Answer: Because of scripture and reasoning. Scripture is as explained before. Reasoning means that someone is a speculator by nature, and so on at length.

items.title: Six Cases of Nihilism, Each Born From Watching Too Little For Too Short a Time

items.zh: 又依世間諸靜慮故，見世施主一期受命恒行布施無有斷絕，從此命終，生下賤家，貧窮匱乏。彼作是思：定無施與、愛養、祠祀。復見有人，一期壽中恒行妙行，或行惡行；見彼命終，墮於惡趣，生諸那落迦，或往善趣，生於天上樂世界中。彼作是思：定無妙行及與惡行，亦無妙行、惡行二業果異熟。
items.en: Relying on worldly meditative concentration, they see a generous donor who practised giving without interruption their whole life, only to die and be reborn into a lowly, impoverished family — and conclude: there is definitely no such thing as giving, caring for elders, or making offerings. They likewise see one person who practised wholesome conduct their whole life die and fall into an unfortunate destiny, one of the hells, while another who practised unwholesome conduct dies and goes to a fortunate destiny, a heavenly world of pleasure — and conclude: there is definitely no such thing as wholesome or unwholesome conduct, nor any ripened result from either.

items.zh: 復見有一剎帝利種命終之後，生婆羅門、吠舍、戍陀羅諸種姓中；或婆羅門命終之後，生剎帝利、吠舍、戍陀羅諸種姓中。吠舍、戍陀羅等，亦復如是。彼作是思：定無此世剎帝利等，從彼世間剎帝利等種姓中來；亦無彼世剎帝利等，從此世間剎帝利等種姓中去。又復觀見諸離欲者生於下地。
items.en: They further see a member of the warrior caste die and be reborn into the priestly, merchant, or labourer caste — or a member of the priestly caste die and be reborn into the warrior, merchant, or labourer caste — and likewise observe those who had achieved freedom from desire nonetheless reborn into a lower realm afterwards, and conclude: there is definitely no continuity at all between "this world" and "that world," no fixed connection carrying any caste or any level of attainment from one life into the next.

items.zh: 又見母命終已，生而為女，女命終已，還作其母；父終為子，子還作父。彼見父母不決定已，作如是思：世間畢定無父無母。
items.en: They see a mother die and be reborn as her own daughter, or a daughter die and be reborn as her own mother; a father die and become his own son, a son become his own father. Having seen the roles of parent and child prove so utterly undetermined, they conclude: the world definitely has no such thing as a true father or mother at all.

items.zh: 或復見人身壞命終，或生無想，或生無色，或入涅槃，求彼生處不能得見。彼作是念：決定無有化生眾生，以彼處所不可知故。
items.en: They further see a person's body perish, and that person be reborn in the non-perception heaven, or in a formless realm, or enter nirvāṇa — and, seeking the place where they were born, cannot see it. They conclude: there are definitely no spontaneously born beings, since their whereabouts cannot be known.

items.zh: 或於自身起阿羅漢增上慢已，臨命終時，遂見生相。彼作是念：世間必無真阿羅漢，如是廣說。問：
items.en: Or someone, having conceived the inflated conceit of having personally attained arhatship, sees, at the moment of their own death, the unmistakable sign of a further rebirth actually arising before them. They conclude: there must be no genuine arhat anywhere in the world at all — and so on in full detail.

blocks.text: Three closely related doctrines: things arise without cause; the self is annihilated at death; and there is no karma, no merit, no arhat at all. All three deny moral causation, and all three, the treatise shows, rest on partial observations, often made in meditation, drawn into hasty conclusions.
Missing from Ru-Yi's translation, now supplied in our own: 0310c29–0311a04 (the seven kinds of annihilationism are named; why outsiders hold it) and 0311a21–a23 (why outsiders hold the empty view).

If things arise without cause, why do they sometimes arise and sometimes not? Why only here and not there? Venerable Miào Jìng cites an example from Master Yìnshùn: "A house on the street catches fire and the fire engines come. Say it arose 'without cause'; would you agree?" He adds: why is one child clever at school and another not? Even when we cannot see a cause, the regularity of the world shows there is one.

The twelfth doctrine: "As long as I possess this coarse body … I am subject to sickness, festering wounds, the arrow of resentment. But once I die, this body is utterly destroyed, like a shattered tile that can never be put back together." Both teachers note the "arrow": resentment towards others, which, Master Cháng Bǎi says, "first strikes yourself". The seven kinds are counted by realm: desire-realm humans and gods (two), form-realm gods (one), and the four formless spheres (four).

The refutation: is it the aggregates that are annihilated, or a self? The aggregates never actually stop; their stream continues. A self was never there. Venerable Miào Jìng adds that the opponent's own words, "I have a body", show the self he clings to has not ended: "If there's a self, there are aggregates; if aggregates, a self."

The thirteenth doctrine has two parts. The first denies the moral world: "There is no such thing as giving, no such thing as caring for one's elders, no such thing as making offerings … up to … no genuine arhat." The second, which tomorrow's reading takes up, denies that anything has any characteristic at all.

The treatise traces the first part to six partial observations, each "born from watching too little for too short a time". A meditator with worldly powers sees a generous person reborn poor, and concludes there is no fruit of giving. Master Cháng Bǎi: "Their absorption is impure and sees little; viewing just two lives, they draw conclusions." But karma may ripen many lives later (Day 7).

Another case: a monk who mistakes the worldly fourth dhyāna for arhatship sees, at death, signs of rebirth arise, and concludes there are no arhats at all. Master Cháng Bǎi, citing the *Vibhāṣā*, tells the story: he slandered nirvāṇa at that moment and fell. The lesson is the same as on Day 44: a real experience in meditation, misread, can be more dangerous than none.

Venerable Miào Jìng adds that the "spontaneously born beings" whom the nihilists deny include not only intermediate beings but those reborn in the heaven of no perception, in the formless realm, and those who enter nirvāṇa: all the destinations an outsider's limited sight cannot follow.

quiz.q: The text refutes the reasoners: uncaused things couldn't sometimes not arise. What example does Venerable Miào Jìng cite from Master Yìnshùn?
options: a house on the street catches fire and the fire engines come — would you agree it arose "without cause"?
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "A house on the street catches fire and the engines come — say it arose 'without cause'; would you agree?" He adds: why is one child clever at school and another slow? Master Cháng Bǎi: wind, rain, flourishing and withering trees all have causes.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what do the annihilationists hold?
options: while the body lasts there is sickness, sores, and arrows; after death it is destroyed and the self is perfectly extinguished
quiz.why: "As long as I possess this coarse body made of the four great elements … I am subject to sickness, to festering wounds, to the sting of resentment. But once I die, this body is utterly destroyed … and at that time I am perfectly, completely extinguished." Master Cháng Bǎi: "After death one is liberated — I'm simply gone."

quiz.q: What image do the annihilationists use for destruction at death?
options: a shattered tile or stone that can't be put back together
quiz.why: "Once my body dies, it is utterly destroyed and ceases to exist — like a shattered tile or stone that can never be put back together." Master Cháng Bǎi: they think karma perishes with the body — a further body would mean results without deeds.

quiz.q: The text asks whether the aggregates or a self are annihilated. For "a self," the translation adds that the earlier descriptions were only ever of the aggregates. How does Venerable Miào Jìng read it differently?
options: by your own words "I have" a body; since the aggregates continue, your self doesn't end either — where there are aggregates there's the self, and vice versa
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Having aggregates shows the self you cling to is still there — it doesn't end. If there's a self, there are aggregates; if aggregates, a self." Master Cháng Bǎi is closer to the translation: "All have form or non-form aggregates as their nature; none is a self — the mark of a self's annihilation can't be found." Both readings refute the view.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what two claims make up the empty-view doctrine?
options: all is suffering; all is impermanent
(1) no giving, caring, offering, up to no true arhat; (2) no phenomenon has any real characteristic
quiz.why: "There is no such thing as giving, no such thing as caring for one's elders, no such thing as making offerings … up to … no genuine arhat"; "further … no phenomenon whatsoever has any real characteristic or nature at all." Master Cháng Bǎi: the first is non-Buddhist; the second, "Mahāyāna wrong-graspers of emptiness."

quiz.q: The text says outsiders, by worldly absorption, see a donor reborn poor and conclude there is no giving. Where does Master Cháng Bǎi say they go wrong?
options: their absorption is impure and limited; seeing only two lives, they conclude — reasoning carelessly from a glimpse
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Their absorption is impure and sees little — viewing just two lives, they draw conclusions"; "seeing a sliver and reasoning carelessly breeds wrong views." Venerable Miào Jìng: "Sometimes those with powers would be better off without them."

quiz.q: The text says one conceited about arhatship sees signs of rebirth at death and concludes there is no true arhat. What story do the teachers cite?
options: the unlearned monk: taking worldly fourth dhyāna for arhatship, at death he saw a rebirth-state arise, slandered the Buddha, and his dhyāna intermediate state vanished, replaced by Avīci's
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi, citing *Vibhāṣā* 69: "attaining the worldly first dhyāna he claimed stream-entry … the fourth, arhatship"; "by the force of slandering nirvāṇa, the fourth-dhyāna intermediate state vanished and Avīci's appeared." Venerable Miào Jìng: the *Śūraṅgama*'s unlearned monk comes from the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
